blocks.content: Subnets divide a VPC's real, foundational network into smaller, real pieces, public and private, spread across genuine, separate availability zones for real resilience.
1. Public vs Private Subnets
A public subnet has real, direct internet access, typically through an internet gateway, a private subnet genuinely does not, by real, deliberate design.
This is a genuinely important, real conceptual distinction, most real, production deployments use both, for different, real, deliberate purposes.
A load balancer typically lives in real, public subnets, while a real database often lives in private ones, genuinely never directly reachable from the internet.
Understanding this distinction well is what makes the rest of this topic's real, practical guidance make sense.
This topic assumes the VPC already covered in the previous topic already genuinely exists, every subnet here lives directly inside it.
Getting this public and private distinction right from the very start avoids a real, later, disruptive reorganization of network structure.

blocks.content: 2. Spreading Across Real Availability Zones
Real subnets, spread deliberately across separate, genuine availability zones, provide real resilience against a single AZ genuinely failing entirely.
The availability_zone argument, or letting AWS choose automatically, determines exactly where a real, specific subnet actually lives.
This directly connects to the Load Balancer topic ahead, which genuinely requires subnets spanning at least two, real, separate AZs.
This real, practical resilience pattern is worth applying by default, not just for genuinely critical, production workloads.
A real, common convention names subnets to include their AZ directly, public_a, public_b, keeping a live layout genuinely easy to navigate.

blocks.alt: Genuine, real resilience, against a single availability zone failing entirely

blocks.content: 3. Subdividing the VPC's CIDR
Recall the VPC's larger, real CIDR block, each subnet claims its own, real, smaller slice of that same, larger address space, genuinely non-overlapping with the others.
Planning this subdivision deliberately, exactly the same real discipline already covered for the VPC's own CIDR choice, avoids a real, later conflict.
A common, real, practical pattern reserves a real /24 block per subnet, within a larger real /16 VPC, genuinely ample for most, real use cases.
This deliberate, upfront planning mirrors the exact same careful thinking already applied to the VPC's own address space.

blocks.content: 4. Route Tables: A Real, Brief Connection
blocks.text: 4. Route Tables: A Real, Brief Connection

blocks.content: A route table determines the real, actual traffic path out of a subnet, an internet gateway route makes a subnet genuinely public, its absence keeps it genuinely private.
This topic introduces the concept briefly, real, complete route table configuration involves several, additional, real resources beyond this topic's core scope.
Understanding this connection is genuinely enough to reason correctly about why a subnet is actually public or private in practice.
A subnet's public or private status comes entirely from its real, associated route table, not from any setting on the subnet resource itself.
This is genuinely worth remembering, a subnet resource itself has no public or private attribute at all, the association is what actually decides it.
This small, real distinction explains a genuinely common early confusion, why marking a subnet public requires more than just naming it that way.

Bringing this topic together, a real, complete subnet layout spans two, genuine availability zones, with both public and private subnets in each, together.
This is worth treating as a genuine, real starting template, the actual foundation the Security Groups and Load Balancer topics ahead build directly on.
This real, four-subnet pattern, two public, two private, across two AZs, is genuinely common in real, production AWS deployments.
Every practice covered in this topic individually comes together here, into one, coherent, real network layout.

blocks.content: 7. NAT Gateways for Private Subnet Access
blocks.text: 7. NAT Gateways for Private Subnet Access

blocks.content: A private subnet needing genuine, real outbound internet access, for software updates, for instance, uses a real NAT gateway, itself living in a public subnet.
This is worth introducing briefly here, a real, common pattern for private resources that still need limited, real, outbound-only connectivity.
A NAT gateway allows real, outbound traffic while still genuinely blocking any unsolicited, real inbound connection from the internet.
This real, asymmetric access pattern is precisely why private subnets remain genuinely secure while still being practically usable.
A NAT gateway genuinely incurs real, ongoing cost, worth weighing directly against the real security benefit it provides for private subnets.
For a genuinely small, non-production environment, a NAT instance, a cheaper, self-managed alternative, is sometimes a real, reasonable tradeoff instead.

blocks.alt: A real, asymmetric pattern, outbound access allowed, inbound access genuinely blocked

blocks.content: 8. A Real, Common Mistake
Placing every subnet in just one, single, real availability zone is a real, common mistake, especially early on, before resilience genuinely matters yet.
This works perfectly fine right up until that one, single AZ has a real, genuine outage, at which point everything in it becomes unreachable together.
The honest fix is spreading subnets across at least two, real AZs from the very start, exactly the pattern already covered earlier in this topic.
This small, real, upfront decision is considerably cheaper than retrofitting multi-AZ resilience onto an already-live, single-AZ deployment later.
